questionText:

"A peasant cultivator named Vithoba from Poona district gave the following testimony before the Deccan Riots Commission in 1876: 'I borrowed Rs. 50 from the Marwari sahukar seven years ago during a drought. I have repaid him more than Rs. 150 in grain and cash over the years. Yet, whenever I ask for my bond back, he claims that the interest has accumulated to Rs. 300. He never gives me a receipt for the grain I deliver. Three years ago, he forced me to sign a blank piece of paper with a stamp on it, saying that under the new Limitation Law of 1859 the old bond had expired. He threatened that if I did not sign, he would obtain a decree from the civil court and auction my bullocks and ancestral land. "A contemporary article published in the Calcutta Review in 1856 analyzed the causes of the bloody Santhal insurrection (Hool): 'The Santhals were invited by the government from the 1830s to settle in the Damin-i-Koh, clear the dense sal forests and bring the land under the plough. The dikus charged exorbitant interest ranging from 50 to 500 percent, manipulated weights and measures, and seized Santhal lands through the collusion of corrupt police darogas.
